name: Qin Shi Huang
info: Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng in 259 BCE, was the king of Qin who conquered the other warring states by 221 BCE, founded the Qin dynasty and became the first emperor of China.

facts.born: February 259 BCE in Handan, capital of the state of Zhao; son of the Qin prince Yiren, later King Zhuangxiang of Qin, and Lady Zhao
facts.died: July or August 210 BCE, at the palace in Shaqiu prefecture during his fifth tour of eastern China, aged 49; the cause is unknown
facts.role: King Zheng of Qin (from 246 BCE, with full power from 235 BCE); First Emperor, Shi Huangdi (221–210 BCE), founder of the Qin dynasty
facts.known: unifying China in 221 BCE; creating the title huangdi, emperor; standardising weights, measures, coinage, axle lengths and script; commanderies and counties in place of the feudal system; the northern walls that preceded the Great Wall; the burning of books; his mausoleum and the Terracotta Army; the search for an elixir of life

t: Between 230 and 221 BCE King Zheng of Qin conquered Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and Qi, ending the Warring States period, and took the new title of huangdi, which Chinese monarchs used for the next two millennia.

With his minister Li Si he replaced the feudal order with commanderies and counties and standardised weights, measures, coinage and script, while mobilising hundreds of thousands of workers for walls, roads, canals and his tomb.

Traditional historiography portrayed him as a brutal tyrant who burned books and buried scholars alive; scholars since the mid-20th century have questioned that picture, which stems partly from the Han dynasty that replaced the Qin.
dyk: After the emperor died on tour, the chancellor Li Si hid the death for the two months' journey back to the capital, ordering carts of rotten fish to travel before and behind the imperial wagon to cover the smell of the body.
ev: Zheng is born in Handan, the capital of Zhao, where his father, the Qin prince Yiren, lives as a hostage
He succeeds his father King Zhuangxiang as king of Qin at the age of 13, with Lü Buwei as regent prime minister
Lao Ai seizes the queen mother's seal and attempts a coup; he is torn to pieces and his family executed to the third degree
Jing Ke, sent by Crown Prince Dan of Yan, tries to stab the king with a dagger hidden in a map and fails
Qin armies capture King Jian of Qi, completing the unification, and Zheng proclaims himself the First Emperor
General Meng Tian routs the Xiongnu from the Ordos Plateau on the emperor's orders
At the instigation of Li Si the emperor orders most existing books to be burned
He dies at Shaqiu on his fifth eastern tour; a forged letter brings his younger son Huhai to the throne as the Second Emperor

sections.early:
According to the Shiji, written by Sima Qian under the Han dynasty, the future emperor was the eldest son of the Qin prince Yiren, who was living at the court of Zhao as a hostage to guarantee an armistice between Qin and Zhao. Yiren had fallen in love with a concubine of Lü Buwei, a rich merchant from the state of Wey, who consented to her becoming the prince's wife; she is known as Lady Zhao. Their son was born in Handan, the capital of Zhao, in 259 BCE, in the first month of the lunar calendar, from which his given name Zheng is said to come. He is called Zhao Zheng in the ancient sources and, more commonly in modern Chinese ones, Ying Zheng, after the ancestral name of the House of Ying.

The Shiji also claims that he was in fact the son of Lü Buwei, the concubine being already pregnant when she was introduced to the prince. The story, widely believed throughout Chinese history, contributed to the generally negative view of the First Emperor, but a number of modern scholars doubt it. Derk Bodde held that the sentence was an interpolation added by an unknown person to slander the emperor, and John Knoblock and Jeffrey Riegel call the story “patently false”. To name a merchant as his father was especially disparaging, since later Confucian society regarded merchants as the lowest social class.

Lü Buwei's machinations helped Yiren become King Zhuangxiang of Qin in 250 BCE. The rulers of Qin had styled themselves kings since 325 BCE, and in 256 BCE King Zhaoxiang of Qin had deposed the last king of Zhou. Qin was at war with the other six states.
sections.rise:
King Zhuangxiang died in 246 BCE after a reign of three years and was succeeded by his 13-year-old son. Because the king was young, Lü Buwei governed as regent prime minister. The king's half-brother Chengjiao, Lord Chang'an, rebelled at Tunliu and surrendered to Zhao; his remaining retainers and their families were executed.

As the king grew older Lü Buwei, fearing that his liaison with the queen dowager would be discovered, found her a replacement in a man named Lao Ai, who according to the Shiji was passed off as a eunuch. Lao Ai and the queen dowager secretly had two sons, and he was made a marquis. In 238 BCE, while the king was travelling to the former capital, Yong, Lao Ai seized the queen mother's seal and raised an army in an attempted coup. The royal army killed hundreds of rebels at the capital. Lao Ai's supporters were beheaded, he was torn into five pieces by horse carriages, his family was executed to the third degree and the two sons were killed; the queen dowager was kept under house arrest until her death. Lü Buwei was banished and in 235 BCE drank poisoned wine. Zheng then assumed full power, and Li Si became chancellor.

In 230 BCE the king began the final campaigns of the Warring States period. Han fell that year, and its king was captured; Handan, the capital of a Zhao weakened by natural disasters, was taken in 228 BCE; the Yan capital Ji fell in 226 BCE; Wei surrendered in 225 BCE after its capital Daliang was besieged and flooded; the Chu capital Shouchun was captured in 223 BCE; and in 221 BCE King Jian of Qi was taken without much resistance.
sections.deeds:
By 221 BCE all the Chinese lands were under Qin. To raise himself above the Zhou kings Zheng created the title huangdi, combining the huang of the mythical Three Sovereigns with the di of the legendary Five Emperors, and took the regnal name First Emperor, expecting his successors to be numbered after him. With Li Si he abolished the feudal system and organised the empire into 36, later 40, commanderies, divided into counties, townships and hundred-family units, with appointments to be based on merit rather than hereditary right.

Weights and measures were standardised, wagon axles given a standard length, the currencies of the states replaced by the Ban Liang coin, and the seal script of Qin made the official standard of writing. Walls between the former states were destroyed, while new walls connected the fortifications of the northern frontier against the Xiongnu; hundreds of thousands of workers were mobilised and an unknown number died. In 215 BCE General Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu from the Ordos Plateau, and campaigns against the Yue annexed regions of modern Guangdong and Vietnam. The Lingqu Canal, begun in 214 BCE and 34 kilometres long, linked the Xiang and Lijiang rivers.

The emperor also built a mausoleum at the foot of Mount Li. Sima Qian wrote that 700,000 men constructed it, a figure the historian John Man doubts as larger than the population of any city of the time. Around 6,000 terracotta statues, found by farmers digging wells in 1974, have been excavated there.
sections.opponents:
Three attempts were made on his life. In 227 BCE Jing Ke, sent by Crown Prince Dan of Yan, came before the king with a map and the severed head of Fan Wuji, stabbed at him with a dagger rolled in the map and missed. Jing Ke's friend, the musician Gao Jianli, later swung a lead-weighted zhu at the king, who had already had his eyes put out, and was executed. In 218 BCE Zhang Liang, a former aristocrat of Han, had a strongman hurl a metal cone weighing 120 jin at the imperial carriage; it shattered the wrong one of two identical carriages.

The emperor eliminated the Hundred Schools of Thought and made Legalism the mandatory ideology. From 213 BCE, at the instigation of Li Si and to prevent scholars from comparing his reign with the past, he ordered most books burned, except those on astrology, agriculture, medicine, divination and the history of Qin. According to the later Shiji, the following year he had some 460 scholars buried alive for possessing forbidden books, an act criticised by his eldest son Fusu. Recent research suggests that this is a Confucian martyrs' legend and that he more probably executed a group of alchemists who had deceived him.

Traditional Chinese historiography almost always portrayed him as a brutal tyrant with an obsessive fear of assassination. The Han statesman Jia Yi, in The Faults of Qin, attributed the collapse to the ruler's lack of “humaneness and rightness”. When a meteor fell at Dongjun in 211 BCE and someone inscribed on it a prophecy of his death, all who lived nearby were put to death.
sections.last:
As he grew old the emperor sought the fabled elixir of life and fell prey to many fraudulent elixirs. He visited Zhifu Island three times in the search, and sent Xu Fu, an islander, with ships carrying hundreds of young men and women to find the mystical Mount Penglai; the expedition never returned. In 212 BCE he began calling himself “The Immortal”. He built tunnels and passageways between his more than 200 palaces, because travelling unseen would supposedly keep him safe from evil spirits.

During his fifth tour of eastern China he fell seriously ill at Pingyuanjin and died in July or August of 210 BCE at the palace in Shaqiu prefecture, about two months' travel from the capital Xianyang, at the age of 49. The cause is unknown, though he had been worn down by his many years of rule; one hypothesis holds that he was poisoned by an elixir containing mercury given to him by his court alchemists and physicians.

Li Si, fearing that the news could set off a general uprising, concealed the death from all but a younger son, Huhai, the eunuch Zhao Gao and five or six favourite eunuchs, and had the emperor's clothes changed and food brought daily as if he were alive. The emperor had never written a will. His eldest son Fusu was first in line, but Li Si and Zhao Gao forged a letter from the emperor commanding Fusu and General Meng Tian, with whom Fusu was in league, to commit suicide. The plan worked, and Huhai began a brief reign as the Second Emperor, Qin Er Shi. The scheme of numbered emperors lasted no longer than this heir, and the Qin were overthrown and replaced by the Han.
sections.legacy:
The title he invented was used by monarchs in China and other countries for two millennia, and the sinologist Michael Loewe writes that few would contest that the achievements of his reign “exercised a paramount influence on the whole of China's subsequent history, marking the start of an epoch that closed in 1911”. His main tomb has not been opened; probes have found mercury at some 100 times the natural rate, which lends credit to parts of Sima Qian's description of rivers of mercury.

His reputation has been repeatedly revised. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when some came to see Confucian tradition as an impediment to China, the Kuomintang historian Xiao Yishan stressed his repulse of the northern peoples, and in 1941 Ma Feibai's biography called him “one of the great heroes of Chinese history” and compared him with Chiang Kai-shek. After 1949 a Marxist critique, set out in the Complete History of China of 1955, held that unification had served the ruling group and the merchant class and that the dynasty's fall showed the class struggle.

Mao Zedong, compared with the First Emperor for his persecution of intellectuals, reportedly boasted in 1958 that he had surpassed him “a hundredfold”. From 1972 an official view presented the emperor as a far-sighted ruler who destroyed the forces of division, and a 1974 article in Red Flag blamed the fall of Qin on the lack of thoroughness of his “dictatorship over the reactionaries”. Since the mid-20th century scholars have questioned the image of the tyrant and strict Legalist.

summary: Qin Shi Huang (259–210 BCE), king of Qin from 246 BCE, conquered the other warring states by 221 BCE and became the first emperor of China. With Li Si he standardised script, coinage and measures and replaced the feudal order with commanderies. Long portrayed as a tyrant who burned books, he has been reassessed since the mid-20th century.
references: Jonathan Clements, The First Emperor of China (Sutton, 2006)
Arthur Cotterell, The First Emperor of China: The Greatest Archeological Find of Our Time (Holt, Rinehart, & Winston, 1981)
Mark Edward Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (Harvard University Press, 2007)
Jane Portal, The First Emperor, China's Terracotta Army (British Museum Press, 2007)
Derk Bodde, China's First Unifier: a Study of the Ch'In Dynasty as Seen in the Life of Li Ssu (280?–208 B.C.) (Hong Kong University Press, 1967)
notes: Death date: the lede gives 12 July 210 BC, the body 'July or August of 210 BC'; the body's wording is used in facts.died and the sections. end -210, not circa.

Assumption of full power: the article says 'Nine years later, in 235 BC' after 246 BC (the arithmetic does not fit), and gives Lü Buwei's banishment and suicide both under 235 BC. The year 235 is kept; 'nine years' left out.
Li Si is called chancellor replacing Lü Buwei in 235 BC; the article gives no further detail.
The second assassination attempt (Gao Jianli) has no date in the article; placed between the dated first and third attempts as the article orders them.

The article has the 460 scholars 'according to the later Shiji' and then 'recent research suggests' a legend; both given. Mao's quoted figures (460, 46,000) and Li Zhisui's '260' are left out except 'a hundredfold'.

Tomb: the article says both that the tomb was 'one of the first projects' of the young king and that in 215 BC he ordered Meng Tian to begin it with 300,000 men, and gives 700,000 (Sima Qian) and 720,000 (other sources); only Sima Qian's 700,000 and John Man's doubt are used.

Twelve statues: heights and weights (5 zhang, 1000 dan) left out. 'Most of the workmen who built the tomb were killed' is stated in the article without attribution; left out for lack of a source line, the editor may want it.
The Great Wall: the article says the Qin walls were a 'precursor to the current Great Wall'; wording kept to 'the northern walls'.
The lede says the southern campaigns added 'Hunan and Guangdong'; the body says 'modern Guangdong and Vietnam'; the body's wording used.
The fall of Qin to the Han is stated only in passing (Names section; Xiang Yu burning Xianyang's palaces in 206 BC); no date for the dynasty's end is given, so none is stated.
Article writes BC; BCE used here.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
